documents: Zhang, Tang & Niu (2022), Earth Planet. Phys. 6(4), 399–423, published PDF including Supplementary Materials (printed pp. 414–423)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (399–423); supplementary pages as S plus a number counted from the supplement's first page (S1 = printed p. 414), with the printed page in parentheses

entry.evidence: What form of iron would produce the observed 3.5−8.8% seismic anisotropy in the western hemisphere of the inner core, given known conditions in the core?

sequences.source_document: Zhang, Tang & Niu (2022), Earth Planet. Phys. 6, 399–423 (published PDF with supplement)

steps.action: The authors take from seismological studies that inner-core P waves travel faster along the polar axis than in the equatorial plane, with a weak eastern and a strong western hemispherical anisotropy.
steps.quote: the eastern hemisphere has a relatively weak anisotropy, of about 0.5−1.5%, whereas the western hemisphere has a strong anisotropy

steps.action: The authors cite the earliest explanation, that crystalline iron is intrinsically anisotropic, as the standing account.
steps.quote: crystalline iron, the main component of the Earth’s inner core, is intrinsically anisotropic

steps.action: The authors pose the question of which form of iron could produce the observed 3.5–8.8% western-hemisphere anisotropy, noting that computed hcp-Fe anisotropies fall short.
steps.quote: What form of iron would produce the observed 3.5−8.8% seismic anisotropy in the western hemisphere of the inner core

steps.action: The authors propose that alloying hcp iron with light elements alters its anisotropy, setting alloys with C, Si, O, S as rivals to pure hcp-Fe; other phases are deferred.
steps.quote: The effect of these light elements on the core’s anisotropy can be explored by assuming that core iron is alloyed with these different light elements.

steps.action: The authors design the study around binary hcp Fe60X4 and Fe56X8 alloys (X = C, O, Si, S), restrict it to the hcp phase, and omit Ni because its effect is cited as negligible.
steps.quote: we focus on the thermoelasticity of hcp-iron alloyed with C, Si, O, and S under inner core conditions.

steps.action: The authors set up DFT-based ab initio molecular dynamics in VASP (PAW, PBE, NVT, Nosé–Hoover thermostat, Mermin electron temperature, blocking-method errors) at 2000, 4000 and 6000 K.
steps.quote: The calculations in this work were performed using density functional theory (DFT) as implemented in the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)

steps.action: The authors test supercell size (64 vs 128 atoms), k-point sampling and run length (up to 10 ps), and fix 64 atoms, 4 irreducible k-points and 8 ps runs.
steps.quote: We ran the AIMD simulations of several structures for up to 10 ps and found that results at higher ps agree

steps.action: The authors derive elastic constants from six finite strains via strain–stress fits, project triclinic tensors to hexagonal, average with Voigt–Reuss–Hill, solve the Christoffel equation, and optimize the finite-temperature c/a for each alloy.
steps.quote: The triclinic tensor can be projected to the hexagonal tensor using the following relationship

steps.action: The authors rely on Li YG et al. (2018), who found projected and directly computed hexagonal constants nearly identical, to support the projection approach.
steps.quote: These results confirm the reliability of the projection approach.

steps.action: The authors compute c/a axial ratios for hcp-Fe and the eight alloys over inner-core pressures at 0–6000 K (Figure 1).
steps.quote: We find that the c/a ratio changes with temperature

steps.action: The authors check the computed c/a of pure hcp-Fe against the Tateno et al. (2010) experiment and earlier calculations, and argue against Sha and Cohen's claim that hcp-Fe is elastically isotropic.
steps.quote: is in close agreement with the experiment of Tateno et al. (2010) (1.602 at 332 GPa and 4820 K)

steps.action: The authors compute densities of Fe and the alloys as functions of pressure and temperature (Figures 2 and 3).
steps.quote: Figure 2 illustrates the changes of the densities of different binary alloys with temperature and pressure

steps.action: The authors compare computed densities with PREM, with the Sakai et al. (2014) experimental extrapolation and with Li YG et al. (2018), and discuss the disagreement on Fe-C melting.
steps.quote: The densities remain higher than PREM data for temperatures not exceeding 6000 K

steps.action: The authors check with root-mean-square displacements and radial distribution functions that the simulated structures remain solid (supplement Text S1, Figure S1).
steps.quote: Both RMSDs and RDFs demonstrate that the simulated structures are solids.

steps.action: The authors estimate light-element contents from the density match to PREM: Si 3.23–6.67 wt.%, S at least 7.55 wt.%, C at most 2.97 wt.% and O at most 3.92 wt.%.
steps.quote: the content of Si in the inner core falls within 3.23−6.67 wt.%

steps.action: The authors compute aggregate compressional velocities of the alloys from 0 to 6000 K at core pressures (Figures 4 and 5).
steps.quote: Figure 4 depicts the variation of the compressional sound velocity (vp) for different binary alloys from 0 K to 6000 K at core pressures.

steps.action: The authors compare vp with PREM and previous AIMD studies, conclude that pure iron cannot match seismology, and attribute differences to averaging, linear fits and potentials.
steps.quote: which means that pure iron cannot alone account for the seismic observations.

steps.action: The authors compare vp from the VRH and Voigt averages (Table S7) and justify choosing VRH.
steps.quote: the vP results based on the VRH average are about 20−200 m/s lower than the vP results based on the Voigt average

steps.action: The authors combine density and velocity results to bound O at 1.4 wt.% and C at 1.8 wt.%, inferring an oxygen-depleted inner core, with Si near 4 wt.% and S near 6 wt.%.
steps.quote: we speculate that the highest contents of oxygen and carbon will not exceed 1.4 wt.% and 1.8 wt.% in the Earth's inner core.

steps.action: The authors test for a relation between c/a and C33/C11 across alloys and temperatures (Figure 6) and find no significant linear relation.
steps.quote: But no significant linear relation exists between the two quantities, and the relation is likely not unique.

steps.action: The authors compute relative P-wave velocity versus angle for Fe and the alloys from their elastic constants, and also from Li YG et al. (2018) constants (Figures 7–9).
steps.quote: Figure 8 presents calculated relative normalized P-wave velocities of the various binary alloys

steps.action: The authors compare the relative-velocity curves with the IMIC model based on Wang et al.'s inner-core anisotropy model.
steps.quote: Nevertheless, we all report values relatively close to the IMIC model based on Wang et al.’s OIC model at high temperatures.

steps.action: The authors compute the anisotropy strength of each alloy across core pressures and temperatures (Figure 10).
steps.quote: The anisotropy strength of relative P-wave velocity at core pressures is presented in Figure [...]

steps.action: The authors attribute the non-monotonic temperature trend (a decrease, then an increase) to a possible artifact of using optimal versus time-averaged structures, not to the alloys.
steps.quote: This phenomenon could be an artifact of the calculation methods

steps.action: The authors compare anisotropy strengths with the 8.8% western-hemisphere maximum (Lythgoe et al., 2014); only Fe60S4 and Fe56S8 exceed it.
steps.quote: only the anisotropy strength of Fe60S4 exceeds 8.8%, the maximum inner core anisotropy at the western region

steps.action: The authors test anisotropy strength under the Voigt, Reuss and VRH averages for Fe60Si4 (Table S6), finding differences of at most 0.002.
steps.quote: In order to exclude the influence of different average methods, the strength of anisotropy of acoustic velocity obtained with different average methods are tested.

steps.action: The authors reject high C or O content as the source of the strong inner-core anisotropy, because these elements decrease anisotropy strength.
steps.quote: This means that high content of C and O elements may not be appropriate to explain the strong anisotropy of inner core.

steps.action: The authors compare their anisotropy strengths at 360 GPa with independent AIMD results of Li YG et al. (2018) and Martorell et al. (Figure 11).
steps.quote: The computed strengths of the anisotropy of hcp-iron and its alloys at 360 GPa are illustrated in Figure 11, in comparison with different AIMD simulations.

steps.action: The authors test the relation between anisotropy strength and c/a (Figure 12) and find only weak linearity, with the alloying element having a strong effect.
steps.quote: only a weak linearity can be detected between elastic anisotropy strength and c/a axial ratio.

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that anisotropy depends jointly on temperature and alloying element: S raises it, C and O lower it relative to Fe at high temperature.
steps.quote: We therefore conclude that the anisotropy depends on combined effects of temperature and the type of alloying element.

steps.action: The authors limit the explanatory claim: Fe-S reaches the required anisotropy but its velocities far exceed PREM, so no binary alloy alone is credited with explaining the anisotropy.
steps.quote: caution is advised in attributing to them, singly or collectively, an explanation of the complex anisotropy of the inner core.

tree.answer: Inner-core seismic anisotropy, stronger in the west (3.5–8.8%), established by cited seismology
No; candidate alloy elasticity at core conditions is computed, not observed
Find whether light-element hcp-Fe alloys can account for the anisotropy magnitude
Pure hcp-Fe versus hcp Fe-X alloys with C, O, Si, S at two concentrations; other phases deferred
Yes; each alloy predicts different density, vp and anisotropy strength
Set in silico (pressure, temperature, composition in AIMD)
Partly: convergence and averaging tests, solidity check, comparison with other AIMD studies
C/O-rich alloys rejected as a strong-anisotropy source; Fe-S passes on anisotropy but fails on velocity; dependence on temperature and element kept

end.claim: Across inner-core pressures and 0–6000 K, the P-wave anisotropy of binary hcp-Fe-X alloys depends on the combined effects of temperature and alloying element: C and O decrease it relative to pure Fe at high temperature, while S significantly increases it, and pressure is a minor factor.

decisive_move.sentence: The finite-temperature AIMD computation of elastic constants, and from them the anisotropy strengths of each hcp-Fe-X alloy at core pressures (Figures 10–11), is the step without which there is no temperature–element dependence to claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the light-element hypothesis chose which alloys to compute (p. 400), but no prediction was stated before the computations. Claim: the alloys' anisotropy strengths could have failed the 8.8% threshold and the PREM density and velocity bounds, and C/O and the Fe-S velocities did fail (pp. 407–412); the headline temperature–element dependence itself faced no test it could fail. Registration: nothing fixed in advance; settings were chosen by balancing cost and reliability (p. 400).

imports.item: Density functional theory (VASP, PAW potentials, PBE GGA)
Nosé–Hoover thermostat NVT molecular dynamics; Mermin finite-temperature electron free energy
Blocking method for error estimates of correlated data (Flyvbjerg and Petersen 1989)
Projector to the closest hexagonal elastic tensor (Moakher and Norris 2006)
Voigt, Reuss and Voigt–Reuss–Hill polycrystal averaging; strain–stress extraction of elastic constants (Page and Saxe 2002)
Adjusted R-square and analysis of variance for linear fits of elastic constants

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgments say reviewers' comments improved the manuscript, but what changed is unknown. The paper makes no explicit 'first' or 'previously unknown' statement; it only states a gap ('a detailed investigation of the anisotropy of hcp-iron alloyed with light elements has been needed', p. 400). Convergence tests (supercell size, k-points, run length) are reported only qualitatively; the 128-atom and 8-k-point results are not shown. The ANOVA of the C44 fits (Text S2, Table S5) is a goodness-of-fit check, not coded as a V check. Only ordered binary alloys in the hcp phase were computed: disordered structures, ternary alloys, other phases and premelting are set aside (pp. 400, 405, 412). The wt.% content bounds carry no stated uncertainty. Sub-claims and their statuses: the light-element content bounds, O ≤ 1.4 wt.% and C ≤ 1.8 wt.% with an oxygen-depleted core (p. 406), are estimate_with_resolution, though weakly, since they are framed as speculation; the rejection of C/O-rich alloys as the source of strong anisotropy (p. 411) is best_explanation; the statement that Fe-S alone reaches 8.8% (p. 412) is offset by its excess velocity and left open. Composition is none_fits (inference): the paper is a computational survey of candidate compositions compared loosely with seismic thresholds (PREM, IMIC, Lythgoe 8.8%). It resembles strong inference in that C/O alloys are excluded, but no crucial test is stated and no single test separates the rivals. The non-monotonic temperature trend of anisotropy is attributed to a possible calculation artifact without a test (p. 407).

disagreements.target: Sha XW and Cohen (2010a, b): hcp-Fe becomes elastically isotropic under inner-core conditions
disagreements.support: Their own AIMD c/a (~1.607 at 360 GPa, 6000 K) stays below the ideal 1.633, and hcp-Fe remains anisotropic.
disagreements.quote: at which hcp-Fe is still substantially anisotropic

disagreements.support: Their computed c/a agrees with experiment and other calculations but is significantly lower than Vočadlo et al.'s; no resolution is offered.
disagreements.quote: although it is significantly lower than the calculation of Vočadlo et al. (2009)

disagreements.target: Li YG et al. (2018): Fe60C4 melts at 5500 K
disagreements.support: Their RDF/RMSD melting criterion shows Fe60C4 and Fe56C8 still solid at 6000 K; they attribute the difference to melting criteria and the NVT versus NPT ensemble.
disagreements.quote: while we find that Fe60C4 and even Fe56C8 are still stable at 6000 K

disagreements.target: Li YG et al. (2018): use of the Voigt average
disagreements.support: They argue the Voigt average overestimates moduli and choose VRH, quantifying the vP difference in Table S7.
disagreements.quote: their calculations use the Voigt average, which calculates polycrystalline elastic moduli based on invariant strain and often overestimates the moduli

disagreements.target: Niu ZW et al. (2015): long-wave limit approximation
disagreements.support: They suggest the long-wave limit approximation underestimates C33/C11 when phonons soften.
disagreements.quote: one possible reason is the underestimation of the C33/C11 ratio, which was obtained on the base of long-wave limit approximation

disagreements.target: Li YG et al. (2018): vp of Fe-C alloys
disagreements.support: Their velocity drops match Li et al. except for the carbon alloys.
disagreements.quote: which is similar to the results of Li YG et al. (2018) with the exception of Fe60C4 and Fe56C8

disagreements.target: Lythgoe et al. (2014): binary hcp-Fe-S alloys have limitations in explaining the western anisotropy
disagreements.support: Their computed Fe-S anisotropy strengths at high temperature are close to or above the 8% maximum estimated by Wang T et al. (2015).
disagreements.quote: Nevertheless, the anisotropy strength of these binary hcp-Fe alloys at high temperatures is close to or more than 8%

disagreements.target: Seismic models explaining inner-core anisotropy by lattice preferred orientation of pure iron
disagreements.support: They argue pure iron cannot produce the observed complexity, citing their vp-PREM mismatch and the anisotropy comparisons.
disagreements.quote: Pure iron alone does not have properties that could explain such complicated anisotropy
